newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD Schroeder wants German campaign debate on EMU.
newsitem.headline: SPD Schroeder wants German campaign debate on EMU.

text.p: A Social Democratic front-runner to challenge Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Germany's 1998 general election said on Monday that Europe's single currency should be a campaign issue next year.

But a survey showed many voters did not want the euro to be debated on the hustings and a leading pollster said Germans seemed happy to let Kohl -- Europe's strongest backer of economic and monetary union (EMU) -- take care of the problem.
Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder said in an interview he was wary of giving up the deutschemark and predicted it would be a focal point of the debate next year.
Such an important issue "cannot be made into a taboo", he told the Neue Ruhr Zeitung. Otherwise, he said, "fears will mount and they will not be calmed".

Schroeder, who clearly leads SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine in popularity polls, has been toying with mildly Euro-sceptical positions as he jockeys for public support in his drive for the party's nomination due to be decided by April 1998.
Lafontaine's few statements on the issue have echoed the majority SPD view that EMU would be so positive for Germany that it cannot be put off.
Kohl's support for EMU is so firm that Germany, where about three-quarters of voters do not want to give up the mark, has had almost no public discussion of the pros and cons of EMU.
President Roman Herzog, who is supposed to be above politics, echoed this recently by calling on politicians to keep the issue out of the 1998 campaign.

Despite all the public concern about giving up the mark, the SPD got a bloody nose when it campaigned in a March 1996 state election for a delay in introducing the euro. Its vote in Baden-Wuerttemberg slumped to its worst ever showing there.
A new opinion poll illustrated the split that results when voters juggle a narrowly focused concern about their money with a broad overall support for European integration.

An Emnid poll for the news magazine Der Spiegel said 56 percent of those surveyed did not want the SPD to make the euro a campaign issue while 42 percent thought it should be debated before the October vote.
But if the SPD opts for a Euro-sceptical platform, the survey showed, a full 81 percent said it should argue for a delay in the 1999 target date for its introduction.
Only 18 percent want the SPD to support a start of the euro as scheduled in January 1999, according to the poll of 1,000 Germans taken on April 2-3.
Dieter Roth, a leading pollster from the Electoral Research Group, said he thought Chancellor Kohl's decision to run for re-election had neutralised EMU as a campaign issue.

"The European currency could have been (a decisive issue) if Kohl had decided not to run," he said. "Now most (voters) will be satisfied that Kohl is managing this. Kohl has very, very high credibility in European affairs."
